misconceptions.statement: The euro is valuable because it is backed by gold.
misconceptions.correction: No major currency is redeemable in gold. Fiat money's value rests on shared acceptance, legal-tender status, and central-bank-managed scarcity.

misconceptions.statement: Money and wealth are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Wealth is everything owned that has value; money is one form of it, and its purchasing power erodes as prices rise.

misconceptions.statement: Keeping cash means taking no risk.
misconceptions.correction: Cash is certain in nominal terms only; it carries purchasing-power risk when prices rise.

misconceptions.statement: Keeping cash costs nothing.
misconceptions.correction: Idle cash forgoes the best alternative's return and loses purchasing power to inflation; zero fees is not zero cost.

misconceptions.statement: Finance is accounting with more mathematics.
misconceptions.correction: Accounting records what happened; finance decides what to do with money across time and risk - different questions on overlapping numbers.

misconceptions.statement: Companies receive money every time their shares trade.
misconceptions.correction: Only primary-market issuance funds the company; secondary-market trades move money between investors.

misconceptions.statement: The stock market is a casino.
misconceptions.correction: Markets trade claims on real businesses and debts; long-run returns come from earnings, not chance.

misconceptions.statement: A low share price means a cheap company.
misconceptions.correction: Price per share means nothing without the share count and the business behind it; value is the whole company against its earnings.

misconceptions.statement: Bonds are safe.
misconceptions.correction: Bonds carry credit risk, interest-rate risk, and inflation risk; 'safer than stocks on average' is not 'safe'.

misconceptions.statement: An index is something you can buy directly.
misconceptions.correction: An index is a calculation, a weighted average of prices; funds that replicate it are what you buy.

misconceptions.statement: Any ETF is diversified by definition.
misconceptions.correction: An ETF is a wrapper; its diversification is exactly that of the index it tracks, which can be one narrow sector or country.

misconceptions.statement: Cash is the no-risk option.
misconceptions.correction: Cash swaps price fluctuation for certain purchasing-power erosion; every option carries some risk, only its kind differs.

misconceptions.statement: Volatility and permanent loss are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Fluctuation reverses; losses become permanent through selling, concentration, or failing businesses.

misconceptions.statement: Owning several funds means being diversified.
misconceptions.correction: Three funds tracking the same market overlap almost completely; diversification is about underlying exposures, not the number of lines.

misconceptions.statement: One or two percent in fees is negligible.
misconceptions.correction: Fees compound against the portfolio every year; over decades one point of annual fees consumes a large share of the final wealth.

misconceptions.statement: Long-term investing means picking winners and waiting.
misconceptions.correction: It means staying broadly invested through cycles so compounding works; concentration plus patience is still concentration.

misconceptions.statement: A good investment is one that went up recently.
misconceptions.correction: Past returns are not evidence about future ones; the decision rests on goal, horizon, cost, risk, and the best alternative.

misconceptions.statement: Prices are set by sellers alone.
misconceptions.correction: A market price balances what sellers offer against what buyers will pay; neither side dictates it for long.

misconceptions.statement: GDP growth means everyone is better off.
misconceptions.correction: GDP measures total production, not its distribution or the wellbeing it buys; averages hide much.

misconceptions.statement: Rate changes act on the economy immediately.
misconceptions.correction: Transmission through borrowing, spending and prices takes quarters to years; policy steers with long lags.

misconceptions.statement: A state budget works like a household budget.
misconceptions.correction: States borrow across generations, issue debt in their own bond market, and their spending feeds back into their own tax base.

misconceptions.statement: Recessions can be predicted and traded around.
misconceptions.correction: Turning points are identified with certainty only in hindsight; cycle-timing strategies reliably lag the data.

misconceptions.statement: A strong currency is always good for the country.
misconceptions.correction: A stronger currency cheapens imports but burdens exporters; the effect depends on which side you are on.

misconceptions.statement: Your broker trades against you.
misconceptions.correction: A plain broker routes your order to the exchange for a fee; it is an access ramp, not your counterparty (products where it IS the counterparty, like CFDs, are a different and riskier business).

misconceptions.statement: Liquidity only matters to big traders.
misconceptions.correction: Every buy and sell crosses the spread, and spreads widen exactly when everyone wants out; liquidity is priced into every trade you make.

misconceptions.statement: There is one price for a share.
misconceptions.correction: There are always two - the bid you sell at and the ask you buy at; the gap is a real trading cost on top of any fee.

misconceptions.statement: A market order executes at the price on your screen.
misconceptions.correction: It executes at whatever the best available opposing price is when it arrives - in thin or fast markets that can be far from the last quote.

misconceptions.statement: A share's price should equal its earnings.
misconceptions.correction: Price is a multiple of expected future earnings; earnings are the annual engine, price the market's valuation of all years to come.

misconceptions.statement: Growth stocks are simply the better companies.
misconceptions.correction: Growth names expected expansion already priced richly; value names low prices on present earnings; each style has led for long stretches, which is why broad indexes hold both.

misconceptions.statement: The coupon rate is the return you get on a bond.
misconceptions.correction: The coupon is fixed to face value; the return depends on the price paid - the yield to maturity captures coupons plus the pull to par on the actual price.

misconceptions.statement: All bonds react equally to rate moves.
misconceptions.correction: Price sensitivity scales with duration: long-maturity, low-coupon bonds move several times more than short ones for the same yield change.

misconceptions.statement: A higher-yielding bond is a better bond.
misconceptions.correction: The extra yield is the priced probability of not being paid; high yield is compensation for credit risk, not free income.

misconceptions.statement: Synthetic ETFs don't really own anything.
misconceptions.correction: A synthetic ETF holds a collateral basket plus a swap contract delivering the index return; the structure differs from physical holding, the exposure and UCITS safeguards remain.

misconceptions.statement: The TER tells you a tracker's full cost.
misconceptions.correction: The realized tracking difference - fund return minus index return - is the true all-in cost; it includes the TER plus trading costs, taxes and lending income, and sometimes beats the TER.

misconceptions.statement: Accumulating and distributing versions of a fund perform differently.
misconceptions.correction: The portfolio is identical; the only difference is whether dividends are paid out or reinvested inside - the choice is about cash needs and taxation, not performance.

misconceptions.statement: Average return tells you how an investment did.
misconceptions.correction: Volatility drags realized growth below the arithmetic average - a +20/-10 sequence averages +5 but compounds to under +4; the money follows the compound path.

misconceptions.statement: Adding a risky asset always makes a portfolio riskier.
misconceptions.correction: An imperfectly correlated risky asset can lower total portfolio volatility - offsetting swings partially cancel; correlation, not the asset's own risk, decides.

misconceptions.statement: The portfolio with the highest return is the best portfolio.
misconceptions.correction: Return per unit of risk is the comparison that matters; a higher return bought with disproportionate volatility is a worse deal, which the Sharpe ratio makes visible.

misconceptions.statement: The right allocation is the one with the highest expected return.
misconceptions.correction: The right allocation is the riskiest mix the investor can hold through a crash without selling - both capacity and tolerance bound it, and an abandoned allocation returns less than a held one.

misconceptions.statement: Risk tolerance and risk capacity are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Tolerance is psychological (what swings you can sleep through); capacity is financial (what losses your situation can absorb given horizon, income and reserves). The allocation must fit the lower of the two.

misconceptions.statement: Tactical shifts to catch market turns add return for skilled amateurs.
misconceptions.correction: Tactical allocation is market timing by another name; the evidence on lessons 25 and 29 applies - mistimed moves cost more than they gain, and the strategic mix does the heavy lifting.

misconceptions.statement: Rebalancing means selling your winners, which lowers returns.
misconceptions.correction: Rebalancing controls risk, not return: it restores the chosen risk level after drift. Its discipline - selling what rose, buying what fell - also removes emotion from the decision.

misconceptions.statement: Portfolios should be rebalanced constantly.
misconceptions.correction: Once a year, or when weights drift past a band such as five points, captures most of the benefit; more frequent trading adds costs and, outside tax wrappers, taxes.

misconceptions.statement: Sequence of returns doesn't matter if the average return is good.
misconceptions.correction: Once money is being withdrawn, early losses are locked in by the withdrawals and cannot be recovered by later gains - the order of returns changes the outcome even at the same average.

misconceptions.statement: A proper portfolio needs many funds.
misconceptions.correction: One broad world-equity ETF plus one high-grade bond fund spans thousands of securities across the main drivers; added funds mostly add overlap, cost and maintenance.

misconceptions.statement: Construction starts with picking good funds.
misconceptions.correction: It starts with the allocation; fund selection is the last step and mostly a cost-and-tracking comparison among near-identical broad products.

misconceptions.statement: Money you might need next year belongs in the portfolio, working.
misconceptions.correction: Near-term money held in volatile assets risks forced selling in a dip - the one scenario that makes losses permanent. Liquidity needs are carved out first, in cash.

misconceptions.statement: Feeling losses strongly is a useful safety instinct for investing.
misconceptions.correction: Loss aversion evolved for physical threats, not markets: it triggers selling after crashes and holding losers - the two moves that convert temporary declines into permanent losses.

misconceptions.statement: Panic selling at least stops the bleeding.
misconceptions.correction: It locks the loss in and adds a second decision - re-entry - that panic sellers systematically make too late, after recovery.

misconceptions.statement: Refusing to sell a loser avoids taking the loss.
misconceptions.correction: The loss already exists at market price; the disposition effect just keeps money in a holding chosen by pride rather than prospects.

misconceptions.statement: Confidence in one's market views is a sign of skill.
misconceptions.correction: Measured calibration shows most investors are overconfident; in markets, confidence without calibration produces more trading, more cost, and worse returns.

misconceptions.statement: Researching a stock you like makes the decision more objective.
misconceptions.correction: Unstructured research feeds confirmation bias - collecting supporting evidence feels like diligence. Objectivity requires actively seeking the case against.

misconceptions.statement: A good story about a company is good evidence about its stock.
misconceptions.correction: Stories are cheap and already priced in; the narrative fallacy sells certainty. Prices move on surprises relative to the story, not on the story itself.

misconceptions.statement: If everyone is buying, they probably know something.
misconceptions.correction: Herds mostly follow prices, not information; buying because others buy is how bubbles inflate, and the crowd's comfort peaks exactly at the top.

misconceptions.statement: Funds with the best recent returns are the best funds.
misconceptions.correction: Past short-run performance barely persists; chasing it means systematically buying after rises - investor returns lag fund returns for exactly this reason.

misconceptions.statement: Missing a boom is as costly as riding a bust.
misconceptions.correction: FOMO prices regret, not risk: a missed gain leaves the plan intact, while a late-entry loss compounds against you. The asymmetry favours the plan.

misconceptions.statement: Investing should start as soon as any money is spare.
misconceptions.correction: Without an emergency reserve, the first surprise forces selling investments at whatever the market then offers; the reserve is what makes long-horizon investing actually long-horizon.

misconceptions.statement: All debt should be cleared before investing anything.
misconceptions.correction: Compare rates: expensive consumer debt beats any expected market return and is repaid first; low-rate mortgage debt can rationally coexist with investing.

misconceptions.statement: Insurance is a savings substitute.
misconceptions.correction: Insurance transfers catastrophic risks that no reasonable reserve could absorb; savings handle the absorbable ones. Insuring small risks or skipping large ones both misprice protection.

misconceptions.statement: The State pension will replace my salary.
misconceptions.correction: French pensions replace only part of net income - typically well under three quarters, less for higher earners and interrupted careers; the gap is what personal saving must fill.

misconceptions.statement: Retirement saving is a concern for one's fifties.
misconceptions.correction: The compounding arithmetic of lesson 5 makes early euros the cheapest: money saved at 25 has twice the compounding runway of money saved at 45.

misconceptions.statement: The PER's tax deduction makes it automatically the best vehicle.
misconceptions.correction: The deduction is deferral, not exemption - exit is taxed and funds are locked until retirement; its value depends on tax rates now versus then, and liquidity has a price.

misconceptions.statement: Taxes on investments are unavoidable, so planning changes little.
misconceptions.correction: Wrapper choice, accumulating funds and low turnover legally change the rate and the timing; over decades the difference compounds like a fee.

misconceptions.statement: Paper gains are taxed each year.
misconceptions.correction: In a CTO, tax falls on realized gains and on distributed dividends; unrealized appreciation compounds untaxed - one reason buy-and-hold and accumulating share classes are tax-efficient.

misconceptions.statement: The flat tax is always 30 percent.
misconceptions.correction: Since January 2026 the PFU is 31.4 percent (12.8 income tax + 18.6 social contributions after the CSG increase), and the progressive scale remains an option worth checking at low marginal rates.

misconceptions.statement: A PEA is an investment; choosing it is choosing what I own.
misconceptions.correction: PEA, CTO and assurance-vie are containers with tax rules; the same world-ETF strategy can live in several of them. Choose holdings first, wrapper by tax and flexibility.

misconceptions.statement: PEA gains become entirely tax-free after five years.
misconceptions.correction: After five years withdrawals are exempt from income tax only; social contributions (18.6 percent since January 2026) remain due on gains.

misconceptions.statement: Assurance-vie is mainly a life insurance policy.
misconceptions.correction: In practice it is a savings wrapper with its own tax clock (advantages from year 8) and succession rules; the insurance element is thin.
